summary:
We developed ROOTWISE AI, a web application that helps small and medium-sized farms decide what to plant, when to plant it, and how to rotate crops. Farmers outline their fields on a map, enter information about soil, water availability, and past crops, and compare options for a proposed planting date.

ROOTWISE AI combines these inputs with five years of regional climate data from NASA POWER. The simulator flags constraints such as frost risk, limited water, and short rotation intervals. It explains what favors or limits each crop, which information is missing, and how much confidence to place in the assessment.

With an initial focus on Peru, ROOTWISE AI aims to help farmers plan around irregular rainfall and water shortages. Farmers can consult previously loaded information and record changes with limited connectivity, then sync those changes when they reconnect.
details:
ROOTWISE AI helps farmers plan planting and crop rotation around the conditions of each field. The farmer draws the field boundary on a map. The application calculates its area and center point, then uses that location to retrieve five years of regional climate data from NASA POWER. Farmers can add soil measurements, elevation, water availability, and crop history. NASA Worldview Snapshots and GIBS imagery give farmers a view of the surrounding area.

The simulator checks critical constraints first, such as historical frost exposure, soil pH outside a crop’s range, or an interval between related crops that is too short. It then evaluates six criteria: climate, soil, water, terrain, planting calendar, and crop rotation. Each crop is classified as recommended, viable with restrictions, high risk, or insufficient information. The application shows the factors behind each result, flags missing information, and displays its confidence in the assessment. It also displays the period and resolution of the NASA climate data so farmers can interpret it at the appropriate regional scale.

The project connects crop comparison with day-to-day farm planning. Farmers can turn a selected option into a growing-season plan, log field work, irrigation, and harvest, and use that history in the next rotation assessment. The intended impact is to help growers choose crops that fit available water and plan rotations that support soil health. The team designed for intermittent connectivity and multilingual access. The application supports previously loaded information and queues supported changes for synchronization. The interface is available in Spanish and English, with beta translations in Runasimi (Quechua), Amazonian Kichwa, and Asháninka.

We built the application with Python, Flask, SQLAlchemy, and SQLite on the backend, and React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS on the frontend. We used Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for mapping, Three.js for 3D visualization, and ReportLab for PDF reports. An optional plant-health feature, AgroVision, uses TensorFlow/Keras and MobileNetV2 to help screen photographs of tomato leaves.
dataRefs: NASA POWER — Historical climate data for the crop simulator
NASA Worldview Snapshots — Satellite imagery around farm fields
NASA GIBS — Satellite imagery layers by date
